summary: Defines an SNMP MIB for watching print jobs. It covers monitoring job status and progress, learning resource needs before a job runs, tracking resource use during printing, and collecting accounting data afterward. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2707 describes a set of SNMP objects for looking inside a printer's job queue. It tells a program what state each job is in, how far it has got, what it needs and what it has used. Everything is read-only, so the MIB can only be watched, never changed.

questions: what is the job monitoring mib
how to monitor print jobs with snmp
what job states does the mib define

subtitle: An SNMP MIB for watching print jobs: what is queued, what is running, and what it cost

tldr.problem: Printers keep their own queues, and the people who submit work to them, the operators who run them and the accountants who bill for them all need to see into those queues in different ways.
tldr.mechanism: The MIB defines four read-only tables. The job table carries a mandatory job state and status for each job, the attribute table carries the rest as numbered attributes that can be added without a new MIB, and a mapping table ties the identifier the client used to the index the agent assigned.
tldr.outcome: The result lets a monitoring program find the busiest printer, follow one job to completion, report errors, and collect the resource usage needed for billing. The memo notes that the IETF published it as an information document and recommends against using it as a model for future MIBs.
tldr.outcomeLabel: What the memo says about itself

facts.label: MIB groups
facts.value: 4: general, job submission ID, job and attribute

facts.value: 4: job set, job, attribute type and attribute instance

facts.value: 8: unknown, pending, pendingHeld, processing, processingStopped, canceled, aborted, completed

today: RFC 2707 is an Informational memo that has not been obsoleted or updated. The IESG note in the document itself recommends against using it as a model for future MIBs, because of the unconventional way it models management information, and the document says it was published for information only rather than as an endorsement of the MIB.

sections.title: What the Job Monitoring MIB Is For
sections.content:
The memo defines an official Printer Working Group standard SNMP MIB for monitoring jobs on network printers. It was published as an IETF Information Document for the convenience of the Internet community, and in consultation with the IETF Application Area Directors it was concluded that the specification properly belongs as an information document, because it monitors a service node on the network rather than a network node proper. The IESG added a note that the MIB uses an unconventional scheme for modelling management information, unique to this MIB, and recommends against using the document as an example for the design of future MIBs.

The MIB is intended to be implemented by an agent inside a printer, or by the first server closest to the printer, and implementations are recommended to place the SNMP agent as close as possible to the processing of the print job. It applies to printers with and without spooling capabilities, and it is designed to be compatible with most commonly used job submission protocols. Where an environment supports high function job submission and job control protocols such as ISO DPA, the memo says those protocols would be used to monitor and manage print jobs instead of this MIB.

The MIB provides four things: monitoring the status and progress of print jobs, obtaining the resource requirements before a job is processed, monitoring resource consumption while a job is being processed, and collecting resource accounting data after a job completes. It is meant to serve several roles. A user wants to identify the least busy printer, to find out the current status of their own job, to get a timely indication that the job has completed and where it can be found, and to see error and diagnostic information for jobs that did not complete. An operator wants a presentation of the state of all jobs in the print system, the identity of the user who submitted each job, the resources each job needs, the choice of which physical printers are candidates, and a rough idea of how long each job will take; no attempt is made to predict exactly how long a job will take. A capacity planner wants printer utilisation as a function of time and how long jobs wait before starting to print. An accountant wants the records needed to charge for resources consumed and to predict consumable usage.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB is aimed at four different readers of the same queue. The person who printed something wants to know if it worked. The operator wants to see everything and decide where to send work. The planner wants to know when the printer will be busy. The accountant wants the bill. The same set of objects serves all four.

sections.title: The Tables and the Attribute Mechanism
sections.content:
The MIB consists of a General Group, a Job Submission ID Group, a Job Group and an Attribute Group, and each group is a table. The General Group holds general information that applies to all jobs in a job set. The Job Submission ID table maps the job submission ID that the client uses to identify a job to the jmJobIndex that the agent uses to identify jobs in the Job and Attribute tables. The Job table holds the mandatory integer job state and status objects. The Attribute table holds multiple entries per job that specify job and document identification and parameters, requested resources, and consumed resources during and after processing.

The job table and the attribute table are indexed first by jmGeneralJobSetIndex, which says which job set, and then by jmJobIndex, which says which job in that set. So that a monitoring application can quickly find the active jobs, which are those in the pending, processing or processingStopped states, the MIB carries two more indexes: jmGeneralOldestActiveJobIndex, the active job that has been in the tables longest, and jmGeneralNewestActiveJobIndex, the active job most recently added. The agent assigns the next incremental value of jmJobIndex to each accepted job, wrapping back to 1 if the implementation-defined maximum would be exceeded, and it is recommended that the largest value be much larger than the number of jobs the implementation can hold, so that an index is not reused while a client still holds a stale value for an older job. When all jobs become inactive the agent sets both active-job indexes to 0.

Attributes are like information objects except that they are identified by an enum rather than an OID, so that attributes can be registered without needing a new MIB, and an implementation that lacks the functionality an attribute represents can omit it entirely rather than having to return a distinguished value. The attribute table has four indexes: the job set, the job, jmAttributeTypeIndex for which attribute, and jmAttributeInstanceIndex for the attributes that can have several values per job. Some attributes describe the job, such as a file name or a submission time; others describe a resource required, such as a medium or a colorant, or the amount of a resource consumed, such as pages completed. Where both a required and a consumed value are needed, the specification assigns two separate attribute enums. An agent should implement an attribute only if the server or device supports what it represents and the information is available to the agent.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything hangs off a job number. The agent hands out job numbers as work arrives and keeps two pointers, to the oldest and the newest job still active, so a program can walk the live jobs without reading the finished ones. Everything else about a job is an attribute, and attributes are numbered rather than named in the object tree, so a new one can be added without a new version of the MIB.

sections.title: The Job State Machine
sections.content:
The mandatory job state is one of eight values, the same as the enum values of the IPP job-state attribute. A job is unknown(2) when its state is not known or is indeterminate, pending(3) when it is a candidate to start processing but is not yet processing, pendingHeld(4) when it is not a candidate for processing for any number of reasons but will return to pending as soon as those reasons are gone, processing(5) while it is being interpreted and printed, processingStopped(6) when processing has stopped part way, and then one of three terminal states: completed(9), canceled(7) or aborted(8). The reasons a job is held are held in the jmJobStateReasons1 object and the jobStateReasonsN attributes for N from 2 to 4, as bits.

Normally a job moves from left to right: it is pending, then processing, and then it finishes. It can be held while pending and released back to pending, and processing can stop and resume. The figure in the memo does not show the transitions to the canceled state from pending, pendingHeld and processingStopped, and the memo says other transitions are unlikely but not forbidden. Jobs in the pending, processing and processingStopped states are called active; jobs in the pendingHeld, canceled, aborted and completed states are called inactive. A job reaches one of the three terminal states after it has completed all activity and all MIB objects and attributes have reached their final values for that job.
sections.plainLanguage: A job starts as a candidate, is held or picked up, is printed, and ends up completed, cancelled or aborted. A job that is waiting, printing or stopped mid-print counts as active; one that is held or finished counts as inactive. Why a job is held is recorded as a set of bits beside the state.

sections.title: Watching a Job Progress
sections.content:
Progress is measured by counting K octets, impressions, sheets and pages, either requested or completed. For impressions and sheets, completed means stacked, unless the implementation cannot detect when each sheet is stacked, in which case stacked is approximated when processing of each sheet completes. There are objects and attributes for the overall job and for the current copy of the document being stacked, and the rate at which they count depends on the sheet and document collation of the job.

Collation is the ordering of work. Sheet collation is the ordering of sheets within a document copy, and document collation is the ordering of document copies within a multi-document job. Three types are defined. UncollatedSheets(3) means no collation of the sheets within each document copy, so each sheet is replicated before the next sheet is processed and stacked; a device with an output bin collator may still produce collated sheets in the bins. CollatedDocuments(4) means the sheets within each copy are collated by making multiple passes over the source or an intermediate representation, and the i'th copy of each document is stacked before the j'th copy of the next document, so a job with documents A and B is delivered as A, B, A, B. If jobCopiesRequested or documentCopiesRequested is 1, the job collation type is defined as 4. UncollatedDocuments(5) means all copies of the first document are stacked before any copy of the next, so the same job is delivered as A, A, ..., B, B.

Four variables are used to monitor the impressions of a job: jmJobImpressionsCompleted, the total number of impressions stacked for the job; impressionsCompletedCurrentCopy, the number stacked for the current document copy; sheetCompletedCopyNumber, the copy number of the current document being stacked, counting from 1; and sheetCompletedDocumentNumber, the document within the job being stacked, counting from 1, which should not be implemented for implementations that support only one document per job. The memo then works through what those four values are for a job with three copies of two documents of three impressions each, once for each of the three collation types.
sections.plainLanguage: The counters say how much of the job is in the output tray. How fast they climb depends on how the job is collated: whether the copies of a page come out together or the pages are repeated one after another. The memo works through an example for each of the three collation types.

sections.title: Identifying a Job
sections.content:
Several attributes let a user, operator or administrator pick out jobs of interest, such as jobURI, jobName and jobOriginatingHost. There is also a jmJobSubmissionID object, which is a text string table index. Being a table index lets a monitoring application find and identify a particular job submitted by a particular client without scanning the whole job table.

The MIB has to identify a job on both sides of the submission process. The client-side identifier is the job submission ID, which can be assigned either by the client's local system or by a downstream server or device, depending on the job submission protocol in use. The server-side identifier, the jmJobIndex, is assigned by the SNMP Job Monitoring MIB agent when the server or device accepts the job. A mapping table links the two, so an application can find the right jmJobIndex in a single Get operation given the job submission ID.

In some configurations more than one application program monitors the same job as it passes from one network entity to another during submission. When there are several job submission IDs, each entity may supply an appropriate one, and there is then a separate entry in the job submission ID table for each, all mapping to the same jmJobIndex that holds the job data; when the job is deleted the agent removes all entries pointing to it. Each registered job submission ID format is a fixed-length 48-octet printable US-ASCII string containing no control characters. The jobName attribute holds a name the user supplied with the job, and it is not necessarily unique, even for one user.
sections.plainLanguage: Two different numbers identify a print job. The client uses its own name for it when it submits the work, and the printer's agent assigns its own number when it accepts the job. A small table maps one to the other, so a program can ask for 'the job I just sent' with a single lookup.

sections.title: Security, Polling and Registration
sections.content:
All objects are read-only, which greatly simplifies the security considerations. If another MIB augments this one and accepts write operations whose effect is to modify the read-only objects here, the memo says that MIB has to support the required access control, not this one. Some sites may want unprivileged users to see only the objects of jobs they submitted, plus a few minimal objects of other jobs, such as jmJobKOctetsPerCopyRequested and jmJobKOctetsProcessed, so that a user can tell how busy a printer is; other sites may let unprivileged users see everything. The MIB neither requires nor specifies how such restrictions would be implemented, and it asks monitoring applications to enforce the site policy when returning information about jobs that do not belong to the user, judged by whether the jmJobOwner object matches the user's name. An operator is a privileged user who sees all objects of all jobs, whatever the policy for unprivileged users.

The MIB specifies no notifications. For simplicity, management applications are expected to poll for status, and the jmGeneralJobPersistence and jmGeneralAttributePersistence objects help an application decide the polling rate; the resulting network traffic is not expected to be significant.

Registration is split between IANA and the Printer Working Group. The PWG registers the enumerations, of three types, the type 2 bit values, the job submission ID formats and the MIME types and sub-types for document formats. The memo also covers internationalisation: text generated by the server or device, text supplied by the job submitter, and the use of DateAndTime for representing date and time.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing here can be changed over SNMP, only read, so the security rules are the site's ordinary ones about who may see whose jobs. There are no alerts either: a program polls for changes, and two objects say how often it needs to poll to catch everything before the printer forgets it.

viz.caption: THE FOUR TABLES OF THE JOB MONITORING MIB

items.title: General Group
items.text: Information that applies to all jobs in a job set, including the oldest and newest active job indexes and the persistence times.

items.title: Job Submission ID Group
items.text: Maps the submission ID the client uses to the index the agent assigned to that job.

items.title: Job Group
items.text: The mandatory integer job state and status objects for each job.

items.title: Attribute Group
items.text: Multiple entries per job: identification and parameters, requested resources, and consumed resources.
